questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to go somewhere where English was the spoken language and then I also included thoughts about the covid-19 situation in my decision process. Additionally, I had heard from older students that Canada was a great country for an exchange stay.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I had a good exchange stay in Canada, but it wasn't without its challenges. In the beginning it was difficult as it was online, and campus was closed etc. - measures that had to be taken because of covid-19. Later when the restrictions lifted it was really fun and interesting. Western is a very social place, but this was limited during my stay, unfortunately.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Upon my arrival campus was closed and everything had to be done via email or going through websites. In my opinion UWO has a lot of different websites pertaining all the different university-related things which can be very confusing. Within the first week where classes also start you have to figure out so many things and that is not easy to do when everything has to be online, so during my stay I didn't find it that easy to find the needed information.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: After a few days the international office had a "zoom-party" with some information, but it was mainly for exchange/international students to "get together" and "meet" each other. It didn't seem like this was the normal procedure and if you're going on exchange in non-pandemic times, I suspect you could expect something different.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: I think the university did what they could when these restrictions were in place. They were available on email and had a day-to-day reply. The orientation about going to Western I thought were missing or not adequate.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Western has about 8 different residences you can apply for. Usually, they use their residences for first-year students so the availability for exchange/other students are limited but if you go in the winter term the odds are higher. I lived in Alumni House which consisted of smaller suites with four rooms, a washroom, and a shared kitchen/living room. I know there are buildings with shared rooms and single rooms but without the kitchen as well.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: In Alumni House there is a kitchen with a stove, microwave, fridge, and freezer, but you can also sign up for the meal plan. Alumni House doesn't have their own dining hall so if on the meal plan you would have to go to another building with a dining hall. The nearest one is just down the street, a little walk of 5 minutes. With a meal plan you can actually go to any residence with a dining hall and eat there. You can also eat at dining halls without a meal plan, but it will be more expensive.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: If living in Alumni House the kitchens are empty besides the bigger items. You would have to buy plates, cups, cutlery, pans, a kettle etc. if you want to be able to cook or eat at home. I was on the meal plan but still bought plates and cups just to be able to cook a cup of coffee or have a snack at home. Being on the meal plan is beneficial as you don't have to spend time cooking and buying groceries (the stores are a bit of a walk/bus ride away) but it is also expensive, and you don't get to choose what you're having in the same way (there is different options but again you didn't choose those options).

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was easy for me to get on campus housing as I went in the winter term, but the interior wasn't too great. The desk and dresser are old, the chair is a mix between a normal chair and a rocking chair, and the couch in the living room is really old and not comfortable. My opinion on this might be worse than others because I had to spend so much time at home and in front of my desk. UWO has many great places for studying on campus but as it was closed throughout January we were forced to sit at home at this strange furniture.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: They have a website with all the courses where you can read three lines about it and then you can continue to a schedule builder to check if any of the courses you wish to take overlap. To me this was really intuitive and great to check if your courses could work together. At the point you're choosing courses not all exam dates are available yet and you won't know if they overlap.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You get an email with a link to the registration page and a description of how to do. As an exchange student we have to do it a little different than the Canadians, so after choosing the courses in the system you have to write the office an email letting them know that you have locked in your choices. They will then put it in the system and let you know if you got a spot or if you would have to find another course.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Besides the description staff are available on email. I found a course that I wanted to register for, but I was unsure if I had the prerequisites. I sent them an email asking whether I would be able to sign up for the course and they replied quick with a useful answer.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Unfortunately, I had some problems with signing up for courses. I began looking at courses I wanted to take shortly after I received their email. When I had decided within the normal registration period, I wrote them an email and they confirmed. Then a month later I received another email asking if I still wanted to come to Western as I hadn't signed up for courses. Apparently, they hadn't locked in my registration properly and I had to choose among the courses that were available in the after registration where the options are more limited. Out of the first four courses I got one and among the three I then chose the second time I got all of them.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Be sure that they have your registration for courses locked in.
If you want to read more about each course, you can find the course description on the faculty's website - it might be the one from last year, but I don't think they change a lot from year to year.
UWO doesn't have a public health program, but they have medical science and health science and the combination of the courses these two programs have is very close to what we have at public health. Both programs don't have many courses that are available for exchange students, unfortunately, but there are some. In addition, you can look at other faculties as there are a lot of relevant courses for a PHS student outside of these two programs.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I had one course that continued online throughout the term which I didn't think was ideal as it was mainly group work. People were more laissez faire when it was online at least in my group, and you don't really get to know people or the group. My three other courses were great, and they got better when the campus opened.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
I had four undergraduate courses, three 4th year and one 3rd year. In my opinion they all had a fair academic level considering everything was in English as well. I did gain some new knowledge, but I also got the chance to use some of the knowledge that I had from UCPH and what I got at UWO in practice as my courses involved doing projects. 
I would like to add that some 4th year Canadians told me that having three module courses (which my 4th year courses apparently were) was a lot of work and that they didn't know anyone doing three module courses at the same time - so be aware of this. I managed well anyway but I do think I had a lot of work and readings throughout the term when comparing with some of the other exchange students.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
In my courses with group work we had some lectures and then also time scheduled to work on the projects. My sociology course was a discussion-based course, so students talked as much - if not even more - than the professor. My economics course was a classic lecture style course where I did miss time put off for trying out the stuff we learned as we had a specific program to work in.
Your grades are a collection of how you did on tests, quizzes, assignments, participation, and the final exam which is a lot different from how we do at PHS. And remember, some courses have mid-terms! I only had one, but it is some to take into consideration and look for when registering for courses.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
EPID 3330G - Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis
EPID 4615B - Health Economic Evaluation
HEALTHSCI 4200G - Advanced Health Promotion
SOCIOLOG 4422G - LGBTQ2S+ Populations

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I really enjoyed the LGBTQ2S+ course as I've learned a lot about those populations as well as Canadian indigenous culture (2S refers to two-spirited which is a thing among the indigenous populations). If you're interested to increase your knowledge about the populations, the living circumstances, and how to do research on them it is a great course. Additionally, this is the discussion-based course, so you really have a great chance to improve your spoken English. As you also get marks on contribution you would have to participate each week, but it is really rewarding. Further, Professor Waite is a really great teacher.
I did not take the course but Canadians from my systematic reviews course told me that 'Major Diseases' is a really great course if you like epidemiology.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I didn't have any unexpected costs.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: When paying for housing and meal plan you pay it all at once and I thought the payment was for a full year and you would get a refund by the end of the term. I only got a refund for the flex money I didn't spend on food (meal plan payment included flex money, I'm not really sure what it meant). This meant that I in total spend 38,000DKK on housing and meal plan which was a lot more expensive than I thought.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: As the pandemic still was present in Ontario non-academic options were limited. I know the university has a big recreational center with a gym and a pool that is available for students. I've heard of clubs, but I don't think they were running in my winter term.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: During my stay we could use the pool and the gym. They also have a peer guide program you can sign up for where you get a Canadian student assigned. They are supposed to help you with whatever questions and queries you have, and they are also a great opportunity if you want to hang out with Canadians.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I enjoyed going to hockey games, both at the university and at the local team (not NHL). The university games are free for students and tickets for the local team are not too expensive.
Apparently, Western University is known for being a party school so the nightlife in London, ON, is busy. It's fun to try out a couple of times. My favorite place was Molly Blooms, which is an Irish pub with karaoke night on Sundays and Mondays. The karaoke culture here is fun as people will get up and dance to people's singing and just support the people up there.
Also, I've heard homecoming (hoco) should be fun as well as foco (fake homecoming). These events take place during the fall. During the winter term there's St. Patrick's Day which is a big thing. People dress up in green and then have house/garden parties and you can just walk in and start talking with people.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: I spent reading week visiting Vancouver and Vancouver Island and it was really fun seeing the west coast as it is different to the east. Some of my friends rented a car and drove to Niagara Falls, Toronto, and Montreal, during reading week. If you have a car available during weekends going to the Falls is easy and I would also recommend going to the lakes. Compared to how big the country is, it is a short drive, and you get to see something else, as London, ON, can be quite boring. I also had the opportunity to go to New York during my stay and after the term I visited Toronto, Ottawa, Montreal, Halifax, and Cape Breton Island (this is a really nice place for hiking). I also went backpacking in Cuba after which takes some preparation, but you can go to the beaches (Varadero) in Cuba for quite cheap without that much preparation.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Quite easy. It looks somewhat similar to Danish culture and as the Canadians are so nice and friendly getting adjusted to the culture is very easy.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: If you take upper year courses (3rd and 4th) the classes are smaller - in my experience between 8 and 30 - which makes it easier to approach local students. Other than that, they are very open and polite, so if you just start a conversation they will respond and participate. I did it in some of my courses as I had some questions and after talking about schoolwork the conversation shifted into a more informal conversation.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: It can be a bit challenging that they're younger. Some of them are really mature but they are in completely different place in life than we are. They are a maximum of 22 years old and only live away from home during the terms. They are not as independent as I think we are in Denmark and sometimes I would take this as a given.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The Canadian friendliness. I always had a feeling of being welcome and appreciated.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) Bring long underwear - it is great when the temperature drops to negative 10-20 degrees and you still have to walk to campus.
2) Don't expect too much of the city. London, ON, is not a great city per se. In my opinion it's a university city that comes to life when the students come back for the term. You basically go downtown for the hockey games, and bars. Other than that, you're mainly just hanging out around campus.
3) Be open to the variety of people you meet. They might seem young and immature, but they can still make great friends and you will learn from each other. This goes both for Canadian students and other exchange students. If you're inclusive in your behavior and are willing to broaden your horizon these people will really add to your exchange experience.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Don't stress too much about deadlines. I experienced that the Canadian students would ask for extension of deadlines all the time, and these were often granted. The professors really want to help and are very accommodating of students' busy schedules. Also, use office hours. I didn't and I regret that. As were not used to office hours in the same way at PHS I didn't know how to use them, but if you're doing projects, they can really help you along the way and make sure the project is headed in the right direction.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The people I've met. Canadians are not necessarily looking for new friends and don't initiate the first conversation - I think this applies for 3rd and 4th year students - but if you do, they will engage, and you would have expanded your network.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The first weeks were rough, and I think it was worsened because of the pandemic and the related restrictions. It was difficult to meet people and the first month had to be spent in our rooms (almost), so it was lonely. Also, because the Canadians stayed at home with their parents to save rent in January. But me and my roomie made some other friends at Alumni which introduced us to some of their friends and so on, so by the end of February my social circle had expanded a lot.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Finding the balance between social life and academic work can be a bit tricky but ask around. Maybe there is some local knowledge on how to do a course or get help from your class mates or TA.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
